label: Capstone
title: Mastery Capstone: Synthesis, Debate Prep & Final Exam
tagline: Five roads, one summit — explaining and defending the whole case
oneSentence: Feser’s five proofs begin from five different undeniable features of reality — change, composition, abstract truths, the gap between what things are and that they are, and the intelligibility of things — and, by one shared two-stage method, each arrives at a cause that must be purely actual, absolutely simple, subsistent existence itself, a necessary intellect and a necessary being; since there can be only one such reality, the five are independent paths to the single God of classical theism, whose nature chapter 6 unfolds and whose critics chapter 7 answers.
bigPicture:
The first nine modules of this course took Feser’s book apart piece by piece. This capstone puts it back together. Its goal is not to add new material but to let you see the book the way its author intends it to be seen: as **one cumulative case** built from five independent demonstrations, a systematic account of the divine nature, and a clearing-away of the standard objections. If you can explain how those pieces fit — why each proof works on its own, why they all land on the same God, what they do and do not claim, and how to answer the twenty objections you are most likely to meet — you have mastered the book.

Three ideas hold the whole thing together. First, **every proof has the same shape**: Stage 1 reasons from an everyday starting point to something that fits a precise description (a purely actual actualizer, an absolutely simple cause, a necessarily existing intellect, subsistent existence itself, a necessary being), and Stage 2 shows that anything fitting that description must be one, unchanging, eternal, immaterial, perfect, good, all-powerful, intelligent and all-knowing. Second, **the four causal proofs are about dependence here and now**, not about a first moment of time: they turn on hierarchical causal series, in which intermediate causes have only borrowed power, and which therefore require an underived source even if the universe had no beginning. Third, **the five descriptions pick out one and the same reality**: whatever is purely actual is simple, whatever is simple is purely actual, both are identical with subsistent existence itself, and all three hold if and only if something exists necessarily — and there cannot in principle be two of any of them.

The capstone is also your final exam and debate lab. You will find a comparison table of the five proofs, a numbered convergence argument, a twenty-item objection handbook drawn from the whole book (with chapter references), a long practice conversation with a sharp skeptic, a 46-question final exam, fourteen essay prompts, fifty flashcards, and an eight-week plan for consolidating everything. Treat it as the place where understanding becomes fluency: you should leave able to pick the right proof for the person in front of you and to defend it without distortion or bluster.

Finally, keep Feser’s own framing in view. He presents these arguments as *demonstrations*, not probabilistic hypotheses; he claims the most common objections rest on misunderstandings; and he insists the real debate is not between atheism and theism but among theists of different kinds, beginning exactly where natural theology leaves off. You do not have to agree with all of that to master the book — but you do need to be able to state it accurately, which is what this capstone trains.
objectives: Describe the two-stage structure shared by all five proofs and explain why it answers the objection that a first cause need not be God.
State each proof’s starting point, key principle, conclusion and characteristic distinction from memory, and reconstruct any one of them step by step.
Explain why the four causal proofs concern hierarchical (per se) causal series operating here and now, and why they are therefore indifferent to whether the universe had a beginning.

Show, using the identity arguments of chapter 6, why the purely actual actualizer, the One, the necessary intellect, subsistent existence itself and the necessary being must be one and the same being.
List at least eight things the proofs do not claim (e.g., that everything has a cause, that the universe began, that God is a being among beings) and correct each misreading.
Summarize how chapter 6 completes the case — proportionate causality, agere sequitur esse, analogy, the divine attributes, conservation, concurrence and miracles.
Answer at least twenty major objections from the whole book, naming the chapter that handles each and anticipating the objector’s follow-up.
Choose and adapt the most suitable proof for different listeners (scientist, mathematician, analytic philosopher, believer, casual skeptic) and present it without the common presentation traps.
Explain what Feser means by a demonstration and why controversy about an argument does not show that it fails.

summary.heading: The book’s project: natural theology without exegesis
summary.body:
Natural theology asks what unaided reason — apart from any claim of divine revelation — can know about whether God exists, what he is like, and how he is related to the world. Feser’s earlier books approached these questions by expounding Aquinas, which meant long stretches of textual interpretation and some seventy pages of general metaphysics before any argument for God appeared. *Five Proofs* deliberately does something else. It offers no exegesis of any historical thinker; it introduces background metaphysics only when an argument needs it; and it defends five arguments, only two of which appear in Aquinas in anything like this form. The proofs are *inspired* by Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Aquinas and Leibniz, and Feser thinks they capture what is essential in those thinkers, but he presents them in his own way and does not claim any of those figures would endorse every detail.

The intended reader is a layperson willing to be eased into abstraction. Feser’s image is of starting in the shallow end of the pool and ending, in every chapter, in the deepest part. Chapters 1–5 each follow the same pattern: an **informal statement** of the argument in two stages, a **more formal statement** in numbered steps (which is not meant to stand alone — it recaps the informal discussion), and a long section of **objections rebutted**, where much of the most technical material lives. Chapter 6 then examines God’s nature and his relationship to the world systematically, and chapter 7 answers the most common objections to natural theology in general.

Feser is openly confident. He argues that the most common objections are feeble and overrated, that what was for most of Western history the mainstream view — that God’s existence can be rationally demonstrated — should be the mainstream view again, and that the real debate is not between atheism and theism but among Jews, Christians, Muslims, Hindus, purely philosophical theists and others. That debate begins where natural theology stops, and the book deliberately does not enter it.

summary.heading: The shared two-stage structure
summary.body:
Every proof is built in two stages. **Stage 1** reasons from some evident feature of the world to the existence of something that fits a precise description:

- Aristotelian: a *purely actual actualizer* (Unmoved Mover).
- Neo-Platonic: an *absolutely simple or noncomposite cause* (the One).
- Augustinian: a *necessarily existing intellect* in which abstract objects exist.
- Thomistic: a cause that is *subsistent existence itself*, whose essence just is existence.
- Rationalist: an *absolutely necessary being*, whose existence is explained by its own nature.

**Stage 2** argues that anything fitting the description must have the key divine attributes: unity (there can be only one), immutability, eternity, immateriality and incorporeality, perfection, full goodness, omnipotence, intellect and omniscience, being the uncaused cause of everything else. Each chapter’s formal statement ends the same way: to exist with these attributes is simply what it is for God to exist.

This structure matters rhetorically and logically. The most common lazy reply to ‘first cause’ arguments is that even if they reach *some* first cause, nothing shows it is God. In Feser’s book that gap is closed inside every chapter, and at greater length in chapter 6. The two stages are one continuous deduction: the attributes are not tacked on by faith but drawn out of the very description Stage 1 establishes.

Note two further common features. Four of the proofs — Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, Thomistic, Rationalist — are *causal* and concern what keeps things in existence **here and now**; the Augustinian proof is not causal at all but starts from the reality of abstract objects. And all five are offered as **demonstrations** — deductions meant to follow necessarily from premises that can be established with certainty — rather than as ‘best explanation’ hypotheses competing with scientific theories.

summary.heading: The common toolkit: concepts the whole book relies on
summary.body:
A handful of ideas introduced early recur everywhere, and fluency with them is most of what mastery requires.

- **Actuality and potentiality.** Change is the actualization of a potential; a potential is neither nothing nor yet actual (the hot coffee really can become cold, but cannot become chicken soup). This answers Parmenides’ worry that change would be something coming from nothing.
- **The principle of causality.** A potential cannot actualize itself; only what is already actual can actualize it. Note what it does *not* say: not that ‘everything has a cause’, only that whatever goes from potential to actual does.
- **Linear vs. hierarchical causal series.** In a linear (per accidens) series — the air conditioner switched on by you, which keeps running after you leave — each member has its own power, and Feser grants such series might extend back infinitely. In a hierarchical (per se) series — cup held up by desk, desk by floor, floor by foundation — every member other than the first has its power only derivatively, like a brush in a painter’s hand. Such a series must have a **first** member, where ‘first’ means *underived*, not *earliest*. Even an infinitely long brush handle could not move itself.
- **The principle of proportionate causality (PPC).** Whatever is in an effect must be in its total cause in some way — formally, virtually or eminently (the $20 bill in my wallet, in my bank account, or in my power to print it). The PPC is what lets Stage 2 infer intellect and omniscience.
- **The principle of sufficient reason (PSR).** Everything is intelligible: there is an explanation for the existence and attributes of whatever exists, found either in the thing’s own nature or in something else. Every cause is an explanation, but not every explanation is a cause, which is why something can be *self-explanatory* without being *self-caused*.
- **The uniqueness argument.** For there to be two of anything, something must distinguish them — a specific difference, a parcel of matter, some perfection one has and the other lacks. Anything so distinguishable has parts or potentiality. Hence there can be only one purely actual, simple, self-existent being.
- **Analogical predication.** Terms like ‘good’, ‘power’ and ‘intellect’ apply to God neither univocally (in exactly our sense) nor equivocally (in an unrelated sense) but analogically — literally, yet not in exactly the same way.

summary.heading: Proof 1 compressed: the Aristotelian proof (chapter 1)
summary.body:
**Starting point:** change is real. The coffee cools, the leaf falls, the puddle grows, the swatted fly dies. Even a lifelong hallucination would involve a succession of experiences, and even arguing that change is illusory involves moving from premise to conclusion. Aristotle’s analysis of change as the actualization of potential defuses Parmenides.

**Key moves.** Any potential that is actualized must be actualized by something already actual. Series of changers stretched through time (coffee cooled by air, air by air conditioner, air conditioner by your finger) might for all the argument cares run back forever — Feser grants a beginningless universe or multiverse for argument’s sake. But every such change presupposes a *thing* that changes, and that thing’s very existence at each moment involves the concurrent actualization of potentials: the water in the coffee exists only because its matter is actually water rather than separate hydrogen and oxygen, which in turn depends on the arrangement of atoms, which depends on subatomic particles, and so on. That is a hierarchical series of actualizers of existence, and it must terminate in something that can actualize without being actualized — something with no potentiality at all, **pure actuality**. It is not merely unmoved but *unmovable*: a ‘first’ actualizer with unactualized potentials would need something further to actualize them and so would not be first.

**Stage 2.** Being purely actual, it cannot change (immutable), so it is outside time (eternal); material things are changeable, so it is immaterial and incorporeal; imperfection and badness are failures to actualize potential, so it is perfect and fully good; there is nothing to distinguish two purely actual beings, so it is unique; all power to actualize derives from it, so it is omnipotent; and since by the PPC the forms of everything it can cause must pre-exist in it — not concretely, as in a cat or a tree, but abstractly, as in a mind — it has intellect and, since nothing is outside its range, omniscience. The formal statement runs to **fifty steps**.

**Signature objections:** ‘What caused God?’ (a straw man — the principle concerns what goes from potential to actual); Hume on conceiving uncaused events; Kant on extending causality beyond experience; Russell’s claim that physics has no causes; Newton’s law of inertia; Einstein’s block universe; quantum indeterminacy and radioactive decay; ‘outdated science’ (Eddington’s two tables); whether hierarchical series are real; and why the mover must be unmovable.

summary.heading: Proof 2 compressed: the Neo-Platonic proof (chapter 2)
summary.body:
**Starting point:** the things of our experience are composite. A chair has legs, screws, seat and cushion; your body has limbs, organs and cells. In one sense the parts are understood through the whole, but in another the whole is less fundamental, because it exists only if its parts exist and are combined in the right way. That dependence is not merely temporal — it holds at every moment, even for something that had always existed or came to be all at once.

**Key moves.** A composite cannot be the cause of its own parts’ being combined; that would be an explanatory vicious circle, the chair lifting itself by its metaphysical bootstraps. So at any moment a composite depends on something else — screws, friction, molecular bonds, a suitable room temperature — and those factors are composite too, yielding a hierarchical series. The principle is completely general: it applies whether the parts are physical (legs, atoms) or metaphysical (form and matter, essence and existence). Such a series must have a first member, and the first member cannot be composite in any way, or it would need a cause itself. So there must be an absolutely **simple or noncomposite** cause — what Plotinus called **the One**.

**Stage 2.** Two simple causes would need a distinguishing feature, which would be a part; so the One is unique. Change means gaining or losing a feature, so it is immutable; it neither begins nor ends, so it is eternal. Using a fourfold division borrowed from William Vallicella — everything is a mind, a mental content, a material thing or an abstract object — the One is not abstract (abstract objects are causally inert), not material (material things have parts), not a mental content (contents depend on minds), so it is a mind or more like a mind than anything else. Having no potential part, it is purely actual, so everything said of the Unmoved Mover applies — and indeed **the One and the Unmoved Mover are identical**. The formal statement has **thirty-eight steps**.

This chapter also introduces two tools crucial later: Frege’s distinction between **sense and reference** (‘morning star’ and ‘evening star’ differ in sense but both name Venus), which explains how God’s many attributes can be one reality; and **analogical predication**, illustrated by the literal but non-identical ‘good’ in ‘good wine’ and ‘good man’. Physics’ wave-particle duality shows we should expect the ultimate level of reality to strain our concepts.

**Signature objections:** a further part might unify the parts (it just adds another item to be unified, regress); unity might be an irreducible or brute fact (either self-causation, which is incoherent, or no explanation at all, not an alternative explanation — and, as Lloyd Gerson notes, the proof has offered one); laws of nature might explain composition (laws plus what they govern are just another composite).

summary.heading: Proof 3 compressed: the Augustinian proof (chapter 3)
summary.body:
**Starting point:** there are abstract objects — universals (redness, triangularity), propositions (what ‘Snow is white’ and ‘Schnee ist weiss’ both express), numbers, and possible worlds (ways things could have been). They exist at least as objects of thought, but they cannot be seen, touched or erased.

**Stage 1 in outline.** Feser gives six direct arguments for **realism** about such objects — the one-over-many argument, the argument from geometry, from mathematics generally, from the nature of propositions, from science, and from possible worlds — plus indirect arguments against the rivals. **Nominalism** (only general words, no universals) faces Russell’s regress (resemblance is itself a universal) and the fact that words are themselves universals (one word type, many tokens). **Conceptualism** (universals are mind-made) cannot explain shared meaning and communication, and **psychologism** undermines itself because any account of how minds build logic must use logic. So some realism is true. But which? **Platonic realism** puts abstract objects in a ‘third realm’ outside minds and matter — yet such objects would be causally inert (so how could we know them, or they explain anything?), would be paradoxically both universal and individual (animality itself would have to be neither rational nor nonrational, which no individual can be), and would make trees and people mere imitations. **Aristotelian realism** — universals exist in things, and as abstract only in minds that abstract them — is better but cannot ground truths and possibilities that would hold even if no material world or human minds existed (pure possibles like unicorns, necessary truths of mathematics). What remains is **Scholastic realism**: abstract objects exist in an infinite, eternal, *divine* intellect.

**Stage 2.** Human, alien and even angelic minds are contingent, so the grounding intellect must exist necessarily. Abstract objects form an interlocking system — grasping one universal requires grasping others, and every proposition stands in logical relations to every other — so they must exist in one intellect that grasps them all, a ‘conceptually omniscient’ being (Robert Adams’ phrase). A necessarily existing intellect must be purely actual (otherwise its existence would depend on something actualizing it), which brings uniqueness and all the other attributes; and if it failed to know some contingent truth it would have unactualized potential, so it is omniscient in the full sense. Greg Welty’s six conditions for a theory of abstract objects (objectivity, necessity, intentionality, relevance, plenitude, simplicity) point the same way. The formal statement has **twenty-nine steps**.

**Signature objections:** divine ideas would not really be ‘abstract’ (begs the question against the Aristotelian understanding of abstraction); Brian Leftow on ‘deity theories’ making God depend on water being H₂O (compare: arithmetic doesn’t depend on rocks); Patrick Grim’s Cantorian argument that there is no set of all truths (proves too much, needs no set, and ignores divine simplicity); and Scholastic critics like Peter Coffey who deny the argument can come *before* God’s existence is known.

summary.heading: Proof 4 compressed: the Thomistic proof (chapter 4)
summary.body:
**Starting point:** for each thing we know, we can distinguish its **essence** (what it is — say, rational animal) from its **existence** (that it is). The question is whether this distinction is merely verbal, like ‘bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’, or real.

**Three arguments for a real distinction.** (1) You can know what a lion, a pterodactyl and a unicorn are without knowing which exists, which is extinct and which never existed; if existence were the same as essence, knowing the essence would reveal the existence. Judging lions not to exist is a false judgment, but it is not a *misconception* of what a lion is, whereas judging a lion not to be a cat would be. (2) Things are contingent; if their existence were identical with their essence, they would exist by nature and could not fail to exist. (3) Something whose essence just is existence could only be one — it could not be differentiated either as a species within a genus or as an individual within a species (each would be ‘existence itself PLUS something’, and so not existence itself) — whereas there are, or could be, many stones, dogs and people. And there is no middle option on which existence is merely one *part* of an essence. A real distinction need not mean separability: the radius and circumference of a circle are really distinct but inseparable.

**Key moves.** A thing whose essence is distinct from its existence cannot give itself existence — it would have to exist before it exists. So its existence must be imparted by something else, and not just when it began but **at every moment**, or it would simply blink out of existence (Fido needs this here and now). If the cause is itself an essence-existence composite, it too needs a cause here and now, generating a hierarchical series that must terminate in something whose essence just *is* existence: what Aquinas calls **subsistent existence itself**.

**Stage 2.** There can be only one such thing; everything else has essence distinct from existence and depends on it; it exists necessarily and is uncaused; essence and existence relate as potency and act, so subsistent existence itself is purely actual — and therefore identical with the Unmoved Mover and possessed of all the attributes. The formal statement has **thirty-six steps**.

**Signature objections:** Hume’s ‘why need a first cause if each member is explained?’ (irrelevant to hierarchical series — an infinite series of IOUs never yields real money; Barry Miller’s point that the explanatory sentence can only be completed by naming a first member); fallacy of composition (not all part-to-whole reasoning is fallacious — Lego — and in any case the argument starts from one thing, not the universe); Anthony Kenny’s two notions of existence (assumes real distinction means separability, and that quantifier-style ‘specific existence’ is the only respectable notion; see John Knasas and Gyula Klima); the aspirin/acetylsalicylic-acid objection that the distinction is merely conceptual (a complete grasp of aspirin’s chemistry would include its being acetylsalicylic acid, but no complete grasp of a lion’s essence ever includes its existence); and doubts about real essences (answered from the unity of natural kinds, the practice of physics described by Nancy Cartwright, Brian Ellis on chemistry, and Crawford Elder’s argument that conventionalism about essence is incoherent).

summary.heading: Proof 5 compressed: the rationalist proof (chapter 5)
summary.body:
**Starting point:** the principle of sufficient reason — everything that exists has an explanation for its existence and its attributes. Everyday life and science always assume it; even unsolved murders have explanations of why they are unsolved.

**Why believe PSR?** Inductively, it is as well confirmed as anything: we find explanations when we look, and a world without PSR would be full of inexplicable events. More decisively, it can be defended by *reductio*. Denying it would mean we have no reason to trust that our perceptions connect to the world (a point from Alexander Pruss and Robert Koons), and — pushing further — no reason to think our beliefs are caused by the good reasons we take ourselves to have, so denying PSR undercuts any grounds for denying it. Explanations that end in a ‘brute fact’ are illusory: a book resting on a shelf that stays up for no reason at all has not really been explained. And Michael Della Rocca shows that critics who use ‘explicability arguments’ elsewhere have no principled, non-question-begging way to exempt the existence of things from them.

**Key moves.** Anything is explained either by another (contingent) or by its own nature (necessary); PSR rules out a third option of being explained by nothing. Contingent things exist. Even if every contingent thing were caused by an earlier one in a beginningless series, universe or multiverse (Hume’s suggestion), the existence of the series itself would remain unexplained — contingency, like the redness of Lego blocks rather than the weight of stones, carries over from parts to collection — and specific features would remain unexplained too (Leibniz’s infinitely recopied geometry book: why *this* content?). Appealing to a contingent cause of the series only starts a higher-order series with the same problem. Alternatively, and without mentioning the universe at all, ask why any single contingent thing persists at this moment; a simultaneous regress of contingent causes can never answer. Only a **necessary being** can end the regress.

**Stage 2.** A necessary being must be purely actual, noncomposite and subsistent existence itself — any potency, parts or essence-existence distinction would make its existence depend on something else. Therefore it is unique and identical with the realities reached by the other proofs. Feser adds that the deep reason things are contingent is that they are act-potency mixtures, composite, and essence-existence composites, and the deep reason they need causes is that otherwise they would be unintelligible. The formal statement has **twenty-seven steps**.

**Signature objections:** ‘rationalism’ implies innate ideas (no — only commitment to intelligibility, understood in a Thomistic way); the ‘big conjunctive contingent fact’ (assumes propositions are Platonic objects needing their own explanation, and that explanation requires logical entailment, which even scientific explanation does not); quantum mechanics (quantum events are made intelligible by quantum laws); ‘why not the universe as the necessary being?’ (it changes and has parts); and ‘What caused God?’ (the rationalist proof makes no exception: God has an explanation, in his own nature).

summary.heading: Why the five converge on one and the same God
summary.body:
A critic might grant each proof and still ask whether they reach five different ultimate realities. Feser answers explicitly in the stage 2 sections and systematically at the start of chapter 6. The key is a set of two-way entailments:

1. **Purely actual ⇔ absolutely simple.** Anything with parts is a mixture of act and potency, because parts only potentially compose the whole until something combines them; so what is purely actual has no parts. Conversely, anything simple cannot have any potency, since it would then have an actual ‘part’ and a potential ‘part’. So the Unmoved Mover (ch. 1) and the One (ch. 2) coincide.
2. **Purely actual ⇔ subsistent existence itself.** Essence and existence relate as potency to act, so a purely actual being cannot have an essence distinct from its existence; and something whose existence depended on actualizing a potency would have derived existence and so not be existence itself. So the ch. 1 and ch. 4 conclusions coincide — and, through step 1, the ch. 2 conclusion as well (a simple being cannot have an essence-existence composition; subsistent existence can have no parts of any kind).
3. **Purely actual, simple, subsistent ⇔ absolutely necessary.** Contingency implies potency to be actualized, parts to be combined, or existence added to essence; and a necessary being can have none of these. So the ch. 5 conclusion coincides with the others.
4. **The necessary intellect is purely actual.** A necessarily existing intellect cannot depend on any actualization, so the ch. 3 conclusion coincides as well — which also explains why the other proofs could infer intellect via the PPC.
5. **There cannot be two.** Any plurality requires differentiation — genus plus specific difference, or form plus matter — and hence parts and potency. So there is, in principle and not merely in fact, only one such being.

The result: the five proofs are ‘distinct paths to one and the same God’, not arguments for five deities. Frege’s morning star/evening star distinction shows why this is not mysterious: ‘purely actual’, ‘simple’, ‘necessary’, ‘subsistent existence’ and ‘supreme intellect’ differ in sense but share a single referent. The convergence also strengthens the case in a non-probabilistic way: each proof is meant to succeed alone, but seeing how their conclusions interlock shows that the attributes are not a grab bag but facets of one idea, and it lets one proof supply what another leaves implicit (for example, the Augustinian proof explains *how* the first cause has intellect).

summary.heading: What the proofs do NOT claim
summary.body:
Most popular criticism attacks arguments Feser never makes. Before defending the case, be able to disown the caricatures:

- **Not that everything has a cause.** The principles are that whatever goes from potential to actual, whatever is composite, or whatever has essence distinct from existence needs a cause; the PSR says everything has an *explanation*, which for God lies in his own nature. Chapter 7 shows that no major defender of cosmological arguments ever used the premise ‘everything has a cause’.
- **Not that the universe had a beginning.** Every causal proof grants, for argument’s sake, a beginningless universe or multiverse. Only the kalām argument (not defended here) tries to prove a beginning.
- **Not a premise about the universe as a whole.** The proofs start from any single thing — a cup of coffee, a stone, Fido. That God causes *everything* is a conclusion, not a premise, so the fallacy of composition charge misfires.
- **Not ‘first’ in time.** The first cause is first in the sense of underived, the source of the borrowed power of every other cause.
- **Not a god of the gaps or a probabilistic hypothesis.** They are demonstrations from starting points any possible empirical theory must presuppose; parsimony and ‘better explanation’ talk does not apply.
- **Not a design argument.** None appeals to complexity, fine-tuning or Paley-style functional order; a pebble or a drop of water would do as a starting point.
- **Not the ontological argument.** God’s necessity is not ‘existence by definition’; Aquinas rejects the ontological argument while accepting the cosmological ones.
- **Not that God is ‘a being’ alongside others.** God is not the biggest item in the inventory, not a member of the genus ‘gods’, but subsistent being itself from which everything else derives its being.
- **Not the truth of any particular religion.** The proofs establish a cause that is one, simple, eternal, omnipotent, omniscient and perfectly good; whether God has revealed himself (the Trinity, prophets, scripture) is a further question.
- **Not that every intelligent hearer will be convinced.** A demonstration is a valid deduction from premises that can be shown true; that people dispute it no more refutes it than disputes refute any other philosophical argument.

summary.heading: How chapter 6 completes the case (I): principles and attributes
summary.body:
Chapter 6 infers from the world, considered as effect, to the nature of its cause, using three background principles. The **PPC** (formally, virtually, eminently) is defended against John Cottingham’s ‘heirloom’ charge and his helium and sponge-cake counterexamples: those concern only material ingredients, not total causes; the principle never required that causes hand on their own form; and even naturalists like Paul Churchland rely on it, while evolution respects it (genes, mutations and environment jointly contain what emerges). **Agere sequitur esse** — action follows being — says what a thing does reflects what it is; even John Searle implicitly uses it against property dualism. The **analogy of being** is defended by showing that potency must have being in a sense analogous to actuality’s (Parmenides and Heraclitus each deny one side incoherently). Analogy comes in two main kinds — of *attribution* (healthy George, healthy food) and of *proper proportionality* (seeing a tree, seeing a theorem) — and both are literal, not metaphorical. Without analogy, talk of God would collapse into anthropomorphism or empty negation.

The attributes then follow:

- **Unity** — including the proof, above, that all five paths reach one God.
- **Simplicity** — nonnegotiable for classical theism (pagans, Jews, Muslims, Christians; Lateran IV and Vatican I; Luther and Calvin). Denying it makes God a ‘superangel’ in need of a cause. Alvin Plantinga’s objection that simplicity makes God a property rests on his broad notion of ‘property’, Platonist view of properties and univocal predication, all rejected by classical theists; Thomas Morris’s necessary-versus-contingent-properties objection is met with Peter Geach’s and Barry Miller’s ‘Cambridge properties’ (God’s being Creator is like Socrates becoming shorter than Plato when Plato grows).
- **Immutability** — acting and being alive do not essentially require being changed; to think otherwise is a **fallacy of accident**.
- **Immateriality and incorporeality**; **eternity** understood as strict timelessness — God causes a whole temporal world in one act, as an author conceives a whole story, and eternity is not a point in time that could be ‘simultaneous’ with Socrates and Obama.
- **Necessity** — not linguistic convention (J. N. Findlay), and not refuted by imagining a world with nothing in it (David Schrader), since God is not imageable and essence determines modality, not the reverse.
- **Omnipotence** — the power to actualize any potential; the stone paradox describes no genuine capacity.
- **Omniscience** — via the PPC and the author analogy; God knows the world by knowing himself as its cause. Foreknowledge no more removes freedom than an author’s writing removes a character’s free choice; God is not a hypnotist inside the story.
- **Perfect goodness** — goodness is actuality relative to a thing’s nature; badness is **privation**, so the PPC does not put evil in God.
- **Will** — free, since nothing outside or inside God compels one creation over another; there is no obligation to create, and no ‘best possible world’.
- **Love** — willing the good of another, which requires no passive emotion.
- **Incomprehensibility** — we know that God is and much of what he is not, and we can speak analogically, but we cannot comprehend him the way we understand things by their parts.

summary.heading: How chapter 6 completes the case (II): God, the world and miracles
summary.body:
The causal proofs imply **divine conservation**: nothing other than God could exist for an instant unless he were sustaining it, so creation is ongoing, not a past event. This rules out ‘existential inertia’ — the idea that things tend to stay in existence on their own — because no composite, act-potency, essence-existence thing could have such a feature, and its defenders never say what would give it one. Because the world is composite, changing and contingent while God is simple, immutable and necessary, the proofs also rule out **pantheism** (God is the world) and **panentheism** (God is changed by the world).

Combining conservation with *agere sequitur esse* yields **concurrence**. **Occasionalism** says only God causes anything; but if creatures truly did nothing, they would not truly exist, and the proofs themselves started from real changes and real composites — occasionalism kicks away the ladder it climbed. **Mere conservationism** says creatures act independently once God keeps them in being; but what cannot exist independently cannot act independently, and the view drifts toward deism. So secondary causes are real but secondary: the chalk makes the square blue, you make there be a square at all; the moon shines, but only with the sun’s light. Human freedom fits like a child whose hand is guided by a parent teaching him to write — the child can resist or cooperate, but the letter appears only with the parent’s guidance.

Finally, **miracles**. On the Aristotelian view, laws of nature describe the tendencies things have by their natures, so they are not broken; a miracle is not a violation but either an *elevation* of nature beyond its own powers or a *suspension* in which God refrains from conserving or concurring with some causes (the three young men unburnt in the furnace). God cannot literally ‘intervene’ in a world that is his own continuous work; better images are the musician improvising beyond the score, the director’s cut, or an author’s second edition. Miracles matter because they would be the rational bridge from natural to revealed theology — the sign that a purported revelation truly comes from God — and natural theology already constrains religions: any that deny God’s unity, distinctness from the world, intellect, will, immateriality or infinite power are thereby shown false.

summary.heading: How chapter 7 completes the case: the objections and their diagnosis
summary.body:
Chapter 7 revisits, from new angles, the objections that have come up throughout and adds several more. Its central diagnosis is historical: the famous ‘basic cosmological argument’ — everything has a cause, so the universe has a cause, God — was never defended by any major proponent, from Plato and Aristotle through Aquinas, Leibniz and Clarke to recent writers; even critic Robin Le Poidevin concedes no one held it. Following W. Norris Clarke, Feser traces the straw man through Russell back to the Mills and ultimately to Hume, who confused the rationalist claim that everything has a *sufficient reason* (Descartes and Spinoza spoke loosely of God as self-caused) with the claim that everything has an *efficient cause distinct from itself*.

The chapter then works through: ‘What caused God?’ (in each proof, the feature that makes things need a cause is precisely what God lacks, so the question asks what caused the uncausable); ‘maybe the universe, Big Bang, multiverse, quantum events or laws are the necessary being’ (each is a mixture of act and potency, composite, contingent; laws are either descriptions, Platonic entities, divine decrees or tendencies of natures, and none is ultimate; and a necessary universe would be pantheism, not atheism); ‘not everything has a cause’ (chance presupposes causal regularities, like the farmer finding buried treasure; quantum events are indeterministic, not unintelligible; Hume’s conceivability test fails); ‘why assume a beginning or a terminus?’; the fallacy of composition (Grayling and Hume are the ones who commit it — sticks, mirrors, Leibniz’s books); ‘why think the first cause is God?’ (Aquinas devoted around a hundred dense pages of the *Summa* to exactly this); ‘this does not prove the Trinity’ (true and irrelevant); Kant’s charge that cosmological arguments presuppose the ontological one (God’s necessity is metaphysical, grounded in pure actuality, not definitional); ‘god of the gaps’ and Lawrence Krauss’s universe ‘from nothing’ (a quantum vacuum and laws of physics are not nothing); **scientism** (self-refuting or trivial; science abstracts from everything unquantifiable, so its success no more shows nothing else exists than a metal detector’s success shows only metal exists; Hume’s fork refutes itself); brute-fact laws (violates PSR, ad hoc, and makes all higher explanations illusory); Dawkins’ ‘the designer is more complex’ (aimed at design arguments; these proofs agree complex things need causes, which is why they conclude to a simple one); ‘one god further’ (a category mistake, like treating triangularity as one more drawn triangle); ‘the God of the philosophers is not the God of religion’ (irrelevant, and false — compare the layman’s crude but real belief in atoms); the problem of evil (Mackie’s logical version fails because some goods — forgiveness, mercy, courage, compassion — logically require evils; Rowe’s evidential version fails against anyone who has independent proof of a good God; an afterlife could outweigh all suffering); divine hiddenness (Schellenberg; most people have in fact believed in the divine); the ‘rationalization’ charge (ad hominem — and Thomas Nagel confessed to hoping there is no God); and ‘it can’t be a proof if so many doubt it’.

summary.heading: Demonstration, controversy and the burden of proof
summary.body:
The book closes by clarifying what it means to call these arguments **demonstrations**. A demonstration, in the classical sense, is a deduction whose conclusion follows necessarily from premises that are certain, where that certainty can be shown by metaphysical analysis. This makes it more secure than a scientific inference in two respects: it is not probabilistic or ‘best explanation’ reasoning where some rival hypothesis might turn out correct, and its premises cannot be overturned by further empirical discovery because they concern what any empirical inquiry presupposes. The Aristotelian proof illustrates this: its starting premise (change occurs) is known through experience, so the argument is not a priori, yet no future experience could overturn it, since any future experience would itself be a change. The other premises (the principle of causality, the impossibility of an infinite hierarchical regress) are defended metaphysically — for instance, the principle of causality follows from PSR, and PSR can be defended by *reductio*.

It follows that controversy is not refutation. Nothing about a demonstration requires that every reader, or even every fair-minded and informed reader, immediately see its force; significant philosophical work may be needed to defend its premises. Feser also notes a double standard: an argument for materialism or against free will is not declared to have ‘failed’ merely because critics exist, yet arguments for God are often treated as dead the moment Hume is mentioned. What a demonstration needs is that, when all is said and done, it can be defended against every objection claiming the premises are doubtful or the conclusion does not follow — which is what the book claims to have done for all five proofs.

For you as a defender, this has practical consequences. Put the burden where it belongs: a critic must show *which* premise is false or *where* the inference fails, not merely gesture at an alternative, a probability or a famous name. And be scrupulous yourself — present the premises accurately, concede what the arguments do not show, and never pass off confidence as proof.

summary.heading: Choosing the right proof for the right conversation
summary.body:
The five proofs are logically independent, so you never need all five at once. (This section is course advice rather than Feser’s text.) Match the entry point to the listener’s existing commitments:

- **Scientists and engineers** usually respond best to the **Aristotelian** proof (everyday change, cups on desks, the difference between how something got here and what keeps it here now) or the **Neo-Platonic** proof (‘what holds this together right now?’). Be ready with the ‘absence from the equations is not absence from reality’ point.
- **Mathematicians, logicians, programmers and Platonist-leaning thinkers** often find the **Augustinian** proof compelling, because they already believe that 2 + 2 = 4 would be true without us. The real work is moving them from Platonism to a divine intellect.
- **People who ask ‘why is there anything at all?’** or who love explanation — including many who know the Leibniz–Clarke tradition from debates — are natural audiences for the **rationalist** proof. Start with PSR and the self-undermining character of denying it.
- **Philosophy students and the metaphysically curious** tend to relish the **Thomistic** proof; its central idea (a thing does not have its existence by its own nature) is the deepest in the book.
- **Believers who think of God as a very powerful person among persons** benefit most from chapter 2 and chapter 6: simplicity, analogy and the category mistake in ‘one god further’.
- **Casual skeptics raised on New Atheist talking points** first need the caricatures removed: no ‘everything has a cause’, no Big Bang premise, no god of the gaps. Often the most persuasive single move is showing that ‘What caused God?’ misunderstands every proof.

Whatever proof you pick, run it through the same five-part checklist: an everyday starting example, the key principle stated precisely, the hierarchical ‘here and now’ point, the Stage 2 attributes, and the one or two objections that listener is likeliest to raise. Then, if the conversation goes well, show how the others converge on the same conclusion — the moment many listeners realize they are not facing a single clever argument but a whole tradition’s worth of converging reasoning.
